title: Using funds generated within the enterprise

blocks.heading: Using funds generated within the enterprise
blocks.text: Retained profit is profit kept in the enterprise rather than distributed to owners. If corresponding cash is available, it can finance equipment, stock or other needs without new outside ownership or loan interest. Retained profit is not automatically a cash balance: money can be tied up in debtors or assets. Selling a surplus asset releases funds, but selling essential equipment can damage capacity. Reducing unnecessary inventory and collecting receivables sooner can release cash already tied up in operations; these actions improve liquidity rather than create fresh sales profit by themselves. Internal sources preserve control and avoid a new finance application, but amounts can be limited and using reserves removes protection against later difficulties. Retained cash has an opportunity cost because it cannot simultaneously finance another project or provide a reserve. Choose the use that best matches the firm’s needs without weakening necessary operations.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Omu Craft has an unused delivery trailer and retained cash, but also needs a reserve for seasonal rent. Selling the unused trailer can release cash without reducing stated current capacity. Using every retained dollar for new tools would leave no rent reserve. Use genuinely spare funds and protect operating needs instead of assuming that internal finance is unlimited or costless.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Finance needs, sources and provider criteria
blocks.text:
Tawa Repairs needs N$60,000 for a machine. It has N$65,000 retained cash after its essential operating reserve and forecasts stable receipts. It compares using that spare cash with a bank loan carrying interest. No alternative use is identified for these spare funds.

Evaluate using Tawa’s spare retained cash instead of borrowing for its machine. Give a concise plan. [12]

Need: long-lived equipment costing N$60,000. Internal option: N$65,000 is genuinely spare after protecting the operating reserve, so cash can meet the stated need without interest or new outside rights. Remaining spare cash would be N$5,000. Borrowing option: preserves additional liquidity and could match equipment benefits, but brings interest and repayment commitments. Provider view: assess repayment cash and risk. Judgement: prefer retained cash on the original facts because funds are available, the essential reserve is already protected and no competing project is identified. Reassess if the supposedly spare funds become necessary elsewhere or cash forecasts deteriorate.
